claim: Nr1d1-/- mice carry an increased proportion of fat mass (24.2 ± 3.0% of body weight) compared to wild type controls (10.8 ± 1.4%)
source: Nr1d1-/- mice are of similar body weight to littermate controls (Figure 1A), yet carry an increased proportion of fat mass (KO: 24.2 ± 3.0% of body weight; WT: 10.8 ± 1.4%; mean ± SEM, p<0.01 Student's t-test, n=12–14/group)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of body composition in Nr1d1-/- mice and wild type controls, with statistical analysis showing p<0.01.

claim: Nr1d1-/- mice display adipocyte hypertrophy when maintained on a standard chow diet
source: Nr1d1-/- mice are of similar body weight to littermate controls (Figure 1A), yet carry an increased proportion of fat mass (KO: 24.2 ± 3.0% of body weight; WT: 10.8 ± 1.4%; mean ± SEM, p<0.01 Student's t-test, n=12–14/group) and display adipocyte hypertrophy (Figure 1B), even when maintained on a standard chow diet.
evidence: The claim is supported by histological examination shown in Figure 1B and stated in the text.

claim: Proteomic profiling of gWAT depots from Nr1d1-/- mice shows deregulation of metabolic regulators and enrichment of metabolic pathways
source: Proteomic profiling of gWAT depots (Nr1d1-/- mice plotted relative to their respective weight-matched littermate controls, n=6/group (C)) shows deregulation of metabolic regulators and enrichment (D) of metabolic pathways (up- and down-regulated proteins shown in blue and red, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in Figure 1C and 1D, showing differential protein expression and pathway enrichment.

claim: The ratio of palmitic to linoleic acid (C16:0/C18:2n6), a marker of de novo lipogenesis, was significantly elevated in Nr1d1-/- gWAT samples
source: To validate this putative increase in local lipid synthesis, we quantified fatty acid species in gWAT, and indeed, the ratio of palmitic to linoleic acid (C16:0/C18:2n6), a marker of de novo lipogenesis, was significantly elevated in Nr1d1-/- samples (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fatty acid profiling data showing increased C16:0/C18:2n6 ratio in Nr1d1-/- samples.

claim: Fatty acid profiling revealed evidence of increased SCD1 activity (C16:1 n-7/C16:0) in Nr1d1-/- gWAT
source: Fatty acid profiling also revealed evidence of increased SCD1 activity (C16:1 n-7/C16:0).
evidence: The claim is supported by fatty acid profiling data showing increased C16:1 n-7/C16:0 ratio.

claim: Nr1d1-/- mice display substantial obesity compared to littermate controls when challenged with 10 weeks of high-fat diet
source: The propensity to lipid storage is further highlighted by the substantial obesity, compared to littermate controls, displayed by Nr1d1-/- mice when challenged with 10 weeks of HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I; Delezie et al., 2012; Hand et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and composition data from HFD-fed mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, and is also supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A strong positive correlation exists between body weight and daily intake of HFD in Nr1d1-/- mice
source: Interestingly, we observed a strong positive correlation between body weight and daily intake of HFD in the Nr1d1-/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J), suggesting that HFD-induced hyperphagia exacerbates weight gain and obesity in the Nr1d1-/- mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Adult Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice did not show an increase in adiposity when maintained on a standard chow diet
source: In marked contrast to global Nr1d1-/- mice, adult Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice did not show an increase in adiposity when maintained on a standard chow diet (Figure 2C; n=7/group), with no differences in mean body weight, fat, and lean mass observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition measurements shown in Figure 2C comparing Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice to controls.

claim: No differences in daily patterns of food intake, energy expenditure, activity levels, or body temperature were observed in matched Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and control mice
source: In parallel with this, we saw no differences in daily patterns of food intake, energy expenditure, activity levels, or body temperature in matched Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and control (Nr1d1Flox2-6) mice (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic phenotyping data shown in Figures 2D-F.

claim: No genotype differences in thermoregulation were observed between Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1Flox2-6 mice
source: However, we saw no evidence of genotype differences in thermoregulation between Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1Flox2-6 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements under various conditions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Despite increased BAT UCP1 expression in the Cre+ve mice, no differences in body temperature profiles were observed between Cre-ve and Cre+ve mice when housed under normal laboratory temperature (22°C) nor when placed under thermoneutral conditions (29°C) for >14 days
source: Despite increased BAT UCP1 expression in the Cre+ve mice, no differences in body temperature profiles were observed between Cre-ve and Cre+ve mice when housed under normal laboratory temperature (22°C) nor when placed under thermoneutral conditions (29°C) for >14 days.
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements and UCP1 expression data under different temperature conditions.

claim: Cre-ve and Cre+ve mice did not differ in their thermogenic response to an acute cold challenge (4°C for 6 hr)
source: Moreover, Cre-ve and Cre+ve mice did not differ in their thermogenic response to an acute cold challenge (4°C for 6 hr) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by body temperature measurements during cold challenge shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: Global Nr1d1 deletion had a large effect on the gWAT transcriptome, with 4163 genes showing significant differential expression (FDR<0.05) between Nr1d1-/- mice and age- and weight-matched WT littermate controls
source: Global Nr1d1 deletion had a large effect on the gWAT transcriptome, with 4163 genes showing significant differential expression (FDR¡0.05) between Nr1d1-/- mice and age- and weight-matched WT littermate controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression in Nr1d1-/- gWAT.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes in Nr1d1-/- gWAT demonstrated that changes are dominated by metabolic genes, with lipid metabolism and the TCA cycle emerging as prominent processes
source: Pathway enrichment analysis demonstrated that these changes are dominated by metabolic genes (Figure 3B), with lipid metabolism and the TCA cycle emerging as prominent processes (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only 231 genes showed significant differential expression between Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1Flox2-6 littermates in gWAT
source: By contrast, and consistent with the absence of an overt phenotype, only a small genotype effect on the transcriptome was observed when comparing gWAT RNA-seq from Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1Flox2-6 littermates (Figure 3C; n=6/group). Here, 231 genes showed significant differential expression between genotypes, of which 126 were also differentially regulated in the WAT analysis of global Nr1d1-/- mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and control mice.

claim: 126 genes were commonly differentially expressed in both Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1-/- gWAT, including circadian clock components (Arntl, Clock, Cry2, Nfil3)
source: Here, 231 genes showed significant differential expression between genotypes, of which 126 were also differentially regulated in the WAT analysis of global Nr1d1-/- mice (Figure 3D). These 126 common genes included circadian clock components (Arntl, Clock, Cry2, Nfil3), whilst pathway analysis also revealed collagen formation/biosynthesis processes to be significantly enriched (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing overlap of differentially expressed genes between the two models.

claim: Pathway analysis of the 126 commonly differentially expressed genes revealed collagen formation/biosynthesis processes to be significantly enriched
source: These 126 common genes included circadian clock components (Arntl, Clock, Cry2, Nfil3), whilst pathway analysis also revealed collagen formation/biosynthesis processes to be significantly enriched (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mouse gWAT exhibits neither enrichment of lipid metabolic pathways nor de-regulation of individual key lipogenic genes previously identified as NR1D1 targets
source: It is notable that Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mouse gWAT exhibits neither enrichment of lipid metabolic pathways nor de-regulation of individual key lipogenic genes, previously identified as NR1D1 targets (Figure 3E,G; Feng et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and pathway analysis, and contrasts with findings from cited previous studies.

claim: Double knockdown of Nr1d1 and Nr1d2 in differentiated 3T3-L1 cells produced greater Arntl de-repression than either Nr1d1 or Nr1d2 knockdown alone, but did not lead to de-repression of lipogenic genes previously considered NR1D1 targets
source: Whilst double knockdown produced greater Arntl de-repression than either Nr1d1 or Nr1d2 knockdown alone, it did not lead to de-repression of lipogenic genes previously considered NR1D1 targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from knockdown experiments in 3T3-L1 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice exhibited greater weight gain and adiposity in response to HFD feeding compared to their controls
source: To test this, Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1Flox2-6 mice were provided with HFD for 16 weeks to drive obesity and WAT expansion. Indeed, compared to their controls, Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice exhibited greater weight gain and adiposity in response to HFD feeding (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and composition measurements during HFD feeding shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Divergence between control and Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice became clear only after long-term HFD feeding (beyond 13 weeks), a time at which body weight gain plateaus in control mice
source: Of note, divergence between control and Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice became clear only after long-term HFD feeding (beyond 13 weeks), a time at which body weight gain plateaus in control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal body weight tracking data during HFD feeding.

claim: HFD-induced hyperphagia is observed in Nr1d1-/- mice (WT food intake 2.92±0.10 g HFD/day/mouse; KO 3.74±0.21 g, p=0.0014) but not in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice (Cre-ve 2.99±0.61 g HFD/day/mouse; Cre+ve 3.01±0.60 g, p>0.05)
source: The stark difference in progression and severity of diet-induced obesity is likely due (at least in part) to the HFD-induced hyperphagia, which is observed in Nr1d1-/- mice (WT food intake 2.92±0.10 g HFD/day/mouse; KO 3.74±0.21 g, p=0.0014, Student's t-test, n=21/genotype), but not in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice (Cre-ve 2.99±0.61 g HFD/day/mouse; Cre+ve 3.01±0.60 g, p>0.05, n=8/genotype).
evidence: The claim is supported by food intake measurements in both mouse models with statistical analysis.

claim: Histological assessment of gWAT after 16 weeks of HFD feeding revealed widespread adipose tissue fibrosis and macrophage infiltration in obese control mice, but these features were not seen in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice
source: Histological assessment of gWAT after 16 weeks of HFD feeding revealed widespread adipose tissue fibrosis (Picrosirius Red staining of collagen deposition under normal and polarised light) and macrophage infiltration (F4/80 immunohistochemistry) in obese control mice, but these features were not seen in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice showed evidence of preserved insulin sensitivity, with neither circulating glucose nor insulin being higher than Nr1d1Flox2-6 littermate controls despite carrying significantly greater fat mass
source: Furthermore, we saw evidence of preserved insulin sensitivity in the HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice, with neither circulating glucose nor insulin being higher than Nr1d1Flox2-6 littermate controls (Figure 4E), despite carrying significantly greater fat mass.
evidence: The claim is supported by blood glucose and insulin measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: On insulin tolerance testing, HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice demonstrated a significantly greater hypoglycaemic response than that observed in HFD-fed controls
source: Indeed, on insulin tolerance testing, HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice demonstrated a significantly greater hypoglycaemic response than that observed in HFD-fed controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No differences in adipocyte size were observed between Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and control genotypes
source: We saw no differences in adipocyte size between the two genotypes, indicating that our observations did not simply reflect greater adipocyte hypertrophy in the Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by adipocyte size quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both gWAT and inguinal white adipose tissue depots (iWAT) were substantially larger in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice than in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6 controls
source: In line with a pronounced increase in fat mass, both gWAT and inguinal white adipose tissue depots (iWAT) were substantially larger in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice than in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6 controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by adipose tissue depot weight measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HFD feeding had a substantial impact on the gWAT transcriptome in both Cre-ve and Cre+ve animals
source: As expected, HFD feeding had a substantial impact on the gWAT transcriptome in both Cre-ve and Cre+ve animals (i.e. NC vs. HFD comparison within each genotype; Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing NC and HFD conditions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Under NC feeding conditions, only a small genotype effect on the transcriptome was observed, with DE genes including core clock genes (Arntl, Nfil3, Npas2, Clock) and those of collagen synthesis pathways
source: Under NC feeding conditions, we again observed only a small genotype effect on the transcriptome, and as before, DE genes included core clock genes (Arntl, Nfil3, Npas2, Clock) and those of collagen synthesis pathways (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing genotypes under NC conditions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Obesity revealed a substantial genotype effect, with 3061 genes DE (1706 up, 1355 down) in HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice vs. HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6 controls
source: However, obesity revealed a substantial genotype effect, with 3061 genes DE (1706 up, 1355 down) in HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice vs. HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6 controls (Figure 5B), and 1704 genes showing a significant (α<0.05) diet-genotype interaction (stageR-specific interaction analysis; Van den Berge et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and interaction analysis comparing genotypes under HFD conditions.

claim: Of 1704 genes showing significant diet-genotype interaction, those up-regulated in obese Nr1d1-deficient adipose were strongly enriched for metabolic pathways, whilst down-regulated genes showed weak enrichment of ECM organisation processes
source: Of these 1704 genes, those up-regulated in obese Nr1d1-deficient adipose were strongly enriched for metabolic pathways, whilst down-regulated genes showed weak enrichment of ECM organisation processes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of genes with diet-genotype interaction shown in Figure 5C.

claim: While HFD feeding caused a profound down-regulation of metabolic pathways in the WAT of control mice, this was not observed in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice
source: While HFD feeding caused a profound down-regulation (vs. NC conditions) of metabolic pathways in the WAT of control mice, this was not observed in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis comparing HFD and NC conditions in both genotypes.

claim: HFD feeding led to an up-regulation of immune pathways in both genotypes
source: HFD feeding led to an up-regulation of immune pathways in both genotypes (Figure 5D); however, as highlighted by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) of differentially regulated genes in gWAT, inflammation and immune-related processes were widely and markedly attenuated in the HFD-fed Cre+ve mice when compared to HFD-fed controls (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Inflammation and immune-related processes were widely and markedly attenuated in the HFD-fed Cre+ve mice when compared to HFD-fed controls
source: HFD feeding led to an up-regulation of immune pathways in both genotypes (Figure 5D); however, as highlighted by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) of differentially regulated genes in gWAT, inflammation and immune-related processes were widely and markedly attenuated in the HFD-fed Cre+ve mice when compared to HFD-fed controls (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by IPA analysis of differentially regulated genes in gWAT.

claim: 4474 ZT8 HaloNR1D1 peaks were identified (MACS2, q<0.01) commonly called against both Halo ZT20 and WT ZT8 libraries
source: We identified 4474 ZT8 HaloNR1D1 peaks (MACS2, q<0.01) commonly called against both Halo ZT20 and WT ZT8 libraries (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq peak calling analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Clear evidence of NR1D1 binding in proximity to core clock genes was observed, with this signal not seen in controls
source: As anticipated, we saw clear evidence of NR1D1 binding in proximity to core clock genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), with this signal not seen in controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing NR1D1 binding near clock genes in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Motif analysis of the high-confidence peak set detected strong enrichment of RORE and RevDR2 motifs
source: Motif analysis of this high-confidence peak set detected strong enrichment of RORE and RevDR2 motifs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), again supporting the specificity of our cistrome.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis of ChIP-seq peaks shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genes commonly up-regulated in NC-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1-/- gWAT are significantly enriched in proximity to HaloNR1D1 ChIP-seq peaks
source: Extending out from NR1D1 ChIP-seq peaks by increasing distances (λ), we found transcription start sites (TSSs) of genes up-regulated in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre and Nr1d1-/- gWAT to be significantly enriched (above all genes in the genome) at distances up to 100 kbp (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing enrichment of up-regulated genes near NR1D1 binding sites.

claim: No enrichment of genes with decreased expression in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre or Nr1d1-/- WAT was evident at any distance from NR1D1 peaks
source: In contrast, no enrichment of genes with decreased expression in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre or Nr1d1-/- WAT was evident at any distance from NR1D1 peaks (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing lack of enrichment for down-regulated genes near NR1D1 binding sites.

claim: HFD-feeding of Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice greatly increased the overlap of DE genes with those DE in Nr1d1-/- WAT
source: HFD -feeding of Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice greatly increased the overlap of DE genes with those DE in Nr1d1-/- WAT (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data from HFD-fed mice shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A highly significant proximity enrichment of commonly up-regulated genes (863) to sites of NR1D1 chromatin binding was observed in HFD-fed mice
source: Critically, we observed a highly significant proximity enrichment of these commonly up-regulated genes (863) to sites of NR1D1 chromatin binding (Figure 6C,D), but again, saw no enrichment of the commonly down-regulated genes (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing enrichment of up-regulated genes near NR1D1 binding sites in HFD conditions.

claim: The large majority of the 863 NR1D1 gene targets unmasked by HFD feeding are normally repressed in obesity, with 551 (63.8%) showing a significant down-regulation in obese control animals
source: Consistent with the healthier metabolic phenotype observed in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice, we found that the large majority of the 863 NR1D1 gene targets unmasked by HFD feeding are normally repressed in obesity (Figure 6E), with 551 (63.8%) showing a significant down-regulation in obese control (Cre-ve) animals (chronic HFD compared to NC-fed state).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression changes in response to HFD feeding shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 495 of the 863 NR1D1 target genes were found to lie within 100 kbp of a NR1D1 binding site
source: Furthermore, 495 of these genes were found to lie within 100 kbp of a NR1D1 binding site (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing proximity of target genes to NR1D1 binding sites.

claim: NR1D1 target genes include important regulators of lipid and mitochondrial metabolism including Fasn, Scd1, Acsl1, Cs, and FGF-21 co-receptor Klb
source: These genes include important regulators of lipid and mitochondrial metabolism (Figure 6F) – including Fasn, Scd1, Acsl1, Cs – and FGF-21 co-receptor Klb, a previously identified NR1D1 target gene (Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by identification of specific genes in the NR1D1 target gene set, with Klb also supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Obesity-dependent de-repression of NR1D1 target genes was also observed in isolated mature adipocytes collected from NC or HFD-fed mice
source: Importantly, obesity-dependent de-repression of these genes was also observed in isolated mature adipocytes (MA) collected from NC or HFD-fed mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data from isolated mature adipocytes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: NR1D1 is a constitutive repressor, with peak expression in the latter half of the inactive phase (daytime in the nocturnal animal)
source: The nuclear receptor NR1D1 (REVERBα) is a core clock component, and has been highlighted as a key link between the clock and metabolism. NR1D1 is a constitutive repressor, with peak expression in the latter half of the inactive phase (daytime in the nocturnal animal).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about NR1D1 function and expression patterns.

claim: In liver, NR1D1 exerts repressive control over programmes of lipogenesis by recruiting the NCOR/HDAC3 co-repressor complex to metabolic target genes
source: In liver, NR1D1 exerts repressive control over programmes of lipogenesis by recruiting the NCOR/HDAC3 co-repressor complex to metabolic target genes, such that global loss of NR1D1 or liver-specific deletion of HDAC3 results in hepatosteatosis (Feng et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015); (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing NR1D1's mechanism of action in liver.

claim: Global loss of NR1D1 or liver-specific deletion of HDAC3 results in hepatosteatosis
source: In liver, NR1D1 exerts repressive control over programmes of lipogenesis by recruiting the NCOR/HDAC3 co-repressor complex to metabolic target genes, such that global loss of NR1D1 or liver-specific deletion of HDAC3 results in hepatosteatosis (Feng et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015); (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NR1D1 regulation of hepatic metabolism is state-dependent, with minimal impact under basal conditions yet increased transcriptional influence in response to mistimed feeding
source: Importantly, we recently showed that NR1D1 regulation of hepatic metabolism is state-dependent, with minimal impact under basal conditions yet increased transcriptional influence in response to mistimed feeding (Hunter et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study by the authors.

claim: Pronounced adiposity and adipocyte hypertrophy are evident in Nr1d1-/- mice, even under normal feeding conditions
source: Indeed, pronounced adiposity and adipocyte hypertrophy are evident in Nr1d1-/- mice, even under normal feeding conditions (Delezie et al., 2012; Hand et al., 2015); (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Daily administration of NR1D1 agonists has been shown to reduce fat mass and WAT lipogenic gene expression in mice
source: Daily administration of NR1D1 agonists has also been shown to reduce fat mass and WAT lipogenic gene expression in mice (Solt et al., 2012), although these agents do have significant off-target actions (Dierickx et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies, with a caveat about off-target effects also cited.

claim: The mammalian circadian clock directs rhythms in behaviour and physiology to coordinate our biology with predictable changes in food availability and daily alternations between fasted and fed states
source: The mammalian circadian clock directs rhythms in behaviour and physiology to coordinate our biology with predictable changes in food availability and daily alternations between fasted and fed states.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about circadian clock function.

claim: A central circadian clock in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) drives daily rhythms in our behaviour and physiology, and orchestrates rhythmic processes in tissue systems across the body
source: A central circadian clock in the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) drives daily rhythms in our behaviour (e.g. sleep/wake cycles) and physiology (e.g. body temperature), and orchestrates rhythmic processes in tissue systems across the body (Dibner et al., 2010; West and Bechtold, 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the SCN and circadian system, supported by citations.

claim: The molecular clock mechanism is present in most cell types
source: The molecular clock mechanism is also present in most cell types.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the ubiquity of molecular clocks.

claim: The rhythmic transcriptome that defines cells and tissues is shaped by both local tissue clock activity and input from the central clock and rhythmic systemic signals
source: The rhythmic transcriptome that defines cells and tissues is shaped by both local tissue clock activity and input from the central clock and rhythmic systemic signals (Guo et al., 2005; Hughes et al., 2012; Kornmann et al., 2007; Koronowski et al., 2019; Lamia et al., 2008; Hunter et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Disturbance of circadian rhythms, as occurs with shift work and irregular eating patterns, is increasingly recognised as a risk factor for metabolic disease and obesity
source: Disturbance of this interaction, as occurs with shift work and irregular eating patterns, is increasingly recognised as a risk factor for metabolic disease and obesity (Broussard and Van Cauter, 2016; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Circadian clock function and its component factors are closely tied into energy metabolism
source: Extensive work over the past 20 years has demonstrated that circadian clock function and its component factors are closely tied into energy metabolism (Bass and Takahashi, 2010; Reinke and Asher, 2019), with strong rhythmicity evident in cellular and systemic metabolic processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles summarizing extensive previous work.

claim: Systemic perturbations such as cancer and high-fat diet feeding can reprogramme circadian control over liver metabolism
source: Clock-metabolic coupling in peripheral tissues is adaptable, as demonstrated by classical food-entrainment studies (Damiola et al., 2000; Mistlberger, 1994), and by recent work showing that systemic perturbations such as cancer and high-fat diet (HFD) feeding can reprogramme circadian control over liver metabolism (Dyar et al., 2018; Masri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Under long-term HFD-feeding conditions, adipose-targeted Nr1d1 deletion results in continued adipose tissue expansion accompanied by a healthier metabolic phenotype with reduced adipose inflammation and fibrosis, and preserved systemic insulin sensitivity
source: Therefore, under long-term HFD-feeding conditions, adipose-targeted Nr1d1 deletion results in continued adipose tissue expansion accompanied by a healthier metabolic phenotype with reduced adipose inflammation and fibrosis, and preserved systemic insulin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The regulatory influence of NR1D1 is context-dependent, with the metabolic impact of adipose-targeted Nr1d1 deletion revealed by transition to an obese state
source: Importantly, these findings also suggest that the regulatory influence of NR1D1 is context-dependent, with the metabolic impact of adipose-targeted Nr1d1 deletion revealed by transition to an obese state.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential effects observed under NC versus HFD conditions.

claim: The healthy adiposity phenotype in HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice results from de-repression of NR1D1-controlled adipocyte pathways which allow continued and efficient lipid synthesis and storage, thus permitting greater expansion of the adipose bed, and attenuation of obesity-related dysfunction
source: Considered together, these findings suggest that the healthy adiposity phenotype in HFD-fed Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice results from de-repression of NR1D1-controlled adipocyte pathways which allow continued and efficient lipid synthesis and storage, thus permitting greater expansion of the adipose bed, and attenuation of obesity-related dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is an inference integrating multiple experimental findings to propose a mechanistic explanation.

claim: NR1D1 is a state-dependent regulator of WAT metabolism, with its widespread repressive action only unmasked by diet-induced obesity
source: We set out to define the role of NR1D1 in the regulation of WAT metabolism and subsequently reveal a new understanding of NR1D1 function. Together, our data show NR1D1 to be a state-dependent regulator of WAT metabolism, with its widespread repressive action only unmasked by diet-induced obesity.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the integration of multiple experimental findings throughout the study.

claim: Nr1d1 expression in WAT appears to limit the energy-buffering function of the tissue
source: Surprisingly, Nr1d1 expression in WAT appears to limit the energy-buffering function of the tissue.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that loss of Nr1d1 allows greater adipose expansion and lipid storage.

claim: Hepatic-selective loss of NR1D1 carries no metabolic consequence, with NR1D1-dependent control over hepatic energy metabolism revealed only upon altered feeding conditions
source: This finding parallels our recent work in the liver (Hunter et al., 2020). Hepatic-selective loss of NR1D1 carries no metabolic consequence, with NR1D1-dependent control over hepatic energy metabolism revealed only upon altered feeding conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study by the authors.

claim: NR1D1 (and potentially other components of the peripheral clock) does not impose rhythmic repression of metabolic circuits under basal conditions but rather determines tissue responses to altered metabolic state
source: Contrary to current understanding, our findings therefore suggest that NR1D1 (and potentially other components of the peripheral clock) does not impose rhythmic repression of metabolic circuits under basal conditions but rather determines tissue responses to altered metabolic state.
evidence: The claim is an inference that challenges current understanding based on the findings of the study.

claim: Under basal conditions, the adipose transcriptional targets under direct NR1D1 control are limited to core clock function and collagen dynamics
source: Taken together, our data suggest that under a basal metabolic state, the adipose transcriptional targets under direct NR1D1 control are in fact limited to core clock function and collagen dynamics.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data under NC conditions.

claim: NR1D1 is not a major repressor of lipid metabolism in basal metabolic state
source: NR1D1 is not a major repressor of lipid metabolism in this setting.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of lipogenic gene dysregulation in adipocyte-specific Nr1d1 deletion under NC conditions.

claim: The enhanced lipid accumulation phenotype of Nr1d1-/- adipose tissue is either independent from adipose NR1D1 entirely or the action of NR1D1 in adipose is context-dependent
source: This also suggests that the enhanced lipid accumulation phenotype of Nr1d1-/- adipose tissue is either independent from adipose NR1D1 entirely or that the action of NR1D1 in adipose is context-dependent.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the discrepancy between global and adipocyte-specific deletion phenotypes.

claim: The broadening of NR1D1's regulatory influence in response to obesity likely reflects a change to the chromatin environment in which NR1D1 operates
source: The broadening of NR1D1's regulatory influence in response to obesity likely reflects a change to the chromatin environment in which NR1D1 operates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference to explain the state-dependent activity of NR1D1.

claim: Emergence of NR1D1's transcriptional control may reflect alterations in chromatin accessibility or organisation, and/or the presence of transcriptional repressors and accessory factors required for full activity
source: Subsequent emergence of NR1D1's transcriptional control may reflect alterations in chromatin accessibility or organisation, and/or the presence of transcriptional repressors and accessory factors required for full activity.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference proposing potential mechanisms for state-dependent NR1D1 activity.

claim: Antagonising WAT NR1D1 emerges as a potential target in metabolic disease
source: Here, we now uncover a role for NR1D1 in limiting the energy-buffering role of WAT, a discovery which may present therapeutic opportunity as we cope with an epidemic of human obesity. Despite recent findings which have cast doubt on the utility of some of the small molecule NR1D1 ligands (Dierickx et al., 2019), antagonising WAT NR1D1 now emerges as a potential target in metabolic disease.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: A functioning circadian clock may be beneficial in coping with acute mistimed metabolic cues but, under chronic energy excess, may contribute to metabolic dysfunction and obesity-related pathology
source: Finally, our study suggests that a functioning circadian clock may be beneficial in coping with acute mistimed metabolic cues but, that under chronic energy excess, may contribute to metabolic dysfunction and obesity-related pathology.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference about the broader implications of the findings for circadian clock function.

claim: The reduced inflammation seen in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice is likely multifactorial, but may be secondary to a reduction in the pro-inflammatory free fatty acid pool, resulting from de-repression of lipogenic and mitochondrial metabolism pathways, or the absence of signals from dead/dying adipocytes
source: The reduced inflammation seen in obese Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice is likely multifactorial, but may be secondary to a reduction in the pro-inflammatory free fatty acid pool, resulting from de-repression of lipogenic and mitochondrial metabolism pathways, or the absence of signals from dead/dying adipocytes.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference proposing potential mechanisms for the reduced inflammation phenotype.

claim: Improved metabolic flexibility is beneficial in other mouse models of metabolic disease and in human obesity
source: It is of note that improved metabolic flexibility is beneficial in other mouse models of metabolic disease (Jonker et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2007; Virtue et al., 2018) and in human obesity (Aucouturier et al., 2011; Begaye et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in both mouse models and humans.

claim: The clock has been linked to ECM remodelling in other tissues, where it is thought to coordinate ECM dynamics, collagen turnover, and secretory processes
source: Whilst the clock has been linked to ECM remodelling in other tissues (Chang et al., 2020; Dudek et al., 2016; Sherratt et al., 2019), where it is thought to coordinate ECM dynamics, collagen turnover, and secretory processes (Chang et al., 2020), we now identify ECM as a direct target of adipose NR1D1 action
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in other tissues.

claim: ECM is a direct target of adipose NR1D1 action
source: Whilst the clock has been linked to ECM remodelling in other tissues (Chang et al., 2020; Dudek et al., 2016; Sherratt et al., 2019), where it is thought to coordinate ECM dynamics, collagen turnover, and secretory processes (Chang et al., 2020), we now identify ECM as a direct target of adipose NR1D1 action
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the identification of collagen genes as direct NR1D1 targets through integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Altered regulation of WAT collagen production and modification likely contributes to the rapid and continued adipose tissue expansion observed in Nr1d1-targeted adipose
source: altered regulation of WAT collagen production and modification likely contributing to the rapid and continued adipose tissue expansion observed in Nr1d1-targeted adipose.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference linking collagen regulation to the adipose expansion phenotype.

claim: The diminished adipose fibrosis seen in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice may reflect alteration in multiple processes, some of which may be under direct/indirect NR1D1 control
source: The diminished adipose fibrosis seen in Nr1d1Flox2-6:AdipoqCre mice may well reflect alteration in multiple processes, some of which may be under direct/indirect NR1D1 control.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference about the mechanisms underlying the fibrosis phenotype.

claim: Adipose-specific deletion of Nr1d1 provides a unique model to explore the complex ECM responses which accompany obesity-related tissue hypertrophy and development of fibrosis
source: Adipose-specific deletion of Nr1d1 thus provides a unique model to explore the complex ECM responses which accompany obesity-related tissue hypertrophy and development of fibrosis.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference about the utility of the mouse model for future research.

claim: A role for the clock in the regulation of WAT function has been reported in the literature
source: A role for the clock in the regulation of WAT function has been reported in the literature (Barnea et al., 2015; Paschos et al., 2012; Shostak et al., 2013), perhaps implying that it is the rhythmicity conferred by the clock which is important for WAT metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Despite robust rhythms of clock genes persisting, rhythmic gene expression in gWAT is largely attenuated following genetic disruption of SCN function
source: However, despite robust rhythms of clock genes persisting, rhythmic gene expression in gWAT is largely attenuated following genetic disruption of SCN function (Kolbe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Metabolic processes, including lipid biosynthesis, were highly enriched in the cohort of SCN-dependent rhythmic genes
source: Indeed, metabolic processes, including lipid biosynthesis, were highly enriched in the cohort of SCN-dependent rhythmic genes from this study (Kolbe et al., 2016), implying that feeding behaviour and WAT responses to energy flux are more important than locally generated rhythmicity for adipose function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study, with an inference about the implications.

claim: A lipogenic phenotype of liver-specific RORα/γ deletion has been shown to be unmasked by HFD feeding
source: Although not explored to the same extent, a lipogenic phenotype of liver-specific RORα/γ deletion has previously been shown to be unmasked by HFD feeding (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In response to HFD feeding, NR1D1 acts to repress metabolic activity in the adipocyte and limit tissue expansion (albeit at the eventual cost of tissue dysfunction, inflammation, and development of adipose fibrosis)
source: Thus, in response to HFD feeding, NR1D1 acts to repress metabolic activity in the adipocyte and limit tissue expansion (albeit at the eventual cost of tissue dysfunction, inflammation, and development of adipose fibrosis).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the integration of multiple experimental findings in HFD-fed mice.

claim: NR1D1 is itself proposed to regulate enhancer-promoter loop formation
source: As NR1D1 is itself proposed to regulate enhancer-promoter loop formation (Kim et al., 2018), modulation of Nr1d1 expression would be a further important variable here.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: With metabolic challenge, emergent circadian rhythmicity is observed in gene expression and in circulating and tissue metabolites
source: Such reshaping of the regulatory landscape likely occurs across tissues, and may explain why, with metabolic challenge, emergent circadian rhythmicity is observed in gene expression (Eckel-Mahan et al., 2013; Kinouchi et al., 2018; Tognini et al., 2017), and in circulating and tissue metabolites (Dyar et al., 2018; Eckel-Mahan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.
